description: We are a dynamic three person team ; Imran, Poyraz, and Ozgun, participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. This is our first NASA Space Apps Challenge except our captain, Imran, this is his 2nd experience in NASA Space Apps. We are here to create a webpage about the story of a NASA Spacecraft. We all know each other for at least a year and we are a very confident team. We believe in our chemistry and skills. We are determined to do a useful project. We are all TED İzmir Highschool Students.
summary: In this project, we developed 3 main things. One of them is a story about the Ingenuity's 72 flight. We wrote as if Ingenuity had feelings and how he was feeling before, after and during his lifetime. The second one is a presentation we made to explain the story and ingenuity, more of a summary of the full story we published at our website . Last but not least, we made a website about the full story. In the webpage firstly we summarized Ingenuity then divided the story into chapters. Firstly, we divided our full story that we published in detail into 4 parts. Then, we made special parts for each.
details:
Drafts:
Here, we wrote the story as a plain text.

They built me out of carbon fiber, off the shelf smartphone processors, and a handful of lithium batteries. While Perseverance, the nuclear powered giant I rode on, was engineered to endure for years, I was built to live thirty days.

​I weighed just four pounds on Earth. On Mars, I felt lighter than a whisper. My entire existence was summed up in two words: technology demonstration. Five flights. Thirty Martian days. Prove that an aircraft could lift itself off the surface of another planet, and then power down forever while Perseverance rolled on to make history.

​When my legs first touched the rusty floor of Jezero Crater in April 2021, I stood alone in a vast, silent desert. Perseverance backed away to a safe distance, watching me with her mast cameras like a nervous parent. The air around me was a near vacuum, one percent as dense as Earth’s. To get off the ground, my four-foot blades couldn't just spin; they had to tear through the thin air at more than 2,500 revolutions per minute, faster than anything that had ever flown back home.

​On Flight 1, I spun up, felt the faint bite of Martian air beneath my rotors, and rose ten feet into the sky. For thirty nine seconds, I hovered the first powered, controlled flight on another world. So called as The “Moment of Wright Brothers”

​By Flight 5, I had checked every box. My mission was over. I was supposed to be shut down right there and then.

​Except a light flickered in me,  I didn't want to stop, and the humans on Earth realized they still needed me. I was their superhero.The moment I was created for, the moment I lived for, the time all eyes were on me. Perseverance was brilliant, but she was heavy and blind to what lay just over the next ridge. I could become her eyes in the sky.

​That was when the real test began. I wasn't designed for a marathon,I wasn’t strong enough, my hands weren’t giving enough.I was still a child in the universe, yet Mars threw every hardship it had at me, as if I were a useless piece of junk.

​First came the dust. Swirling red grit coated my solar panel, starving my batteries of the sunlight I needed to survive. Then came the Martian winter. Temperatures plunged to minus 112 degrees Fahrenheit in the pitch dark. Without enough power to run my internal heaters, I couldn't fight off the cold. Every single night, I froze solid. My processor shut down. My clock reset to zero. Every night, I died a little death in the dark, and every morning, when the first rays of sun hit my dusty solar array, I thawed out, booted back up, and pinged Perseverance to let her know I was ready to fly again.

​In May 2022, my inclinometer, the sensor that told me which way was up, failed permanently. I was blind to my own tilt. The engineers a hundred million miles away rewrote my flight software on the fly, teaching me to use my other instruments to guess my balance before taking off.I adapted to the difficulties as I was  a creation to climb myself to perfectness.

​Five flights became twenty. Twenty became fifty.The numbers were adding up , I was developing against the difficulties. I scouted treacherous, lethal  boulder fields, leaped across ancient riverbeds, and flew higher and faster than my designers ever dared to dream.

​By January 2024, I had flown seventy one times. I had survived nearly three Earth years on a thirty day warranty. Everything was wonderful.I thought that nothing would go wrong.

​Then came Flight 72.

​I rose above a stretch of smooth, featureless sand ripples in Neretva Vallis, Not aware of the things that were about to occur. My navigation camera which was looking downward searched the ground for rocks or shadows to lock onto so I could track my position and found nothing. Just endless, uniform waves of sand. Without a visual anchor, my software lost its grip on where I was heading towards.

​I came down hard. As my landing legs struck the slope, one of my carbon fiber rotor blades clipped the sand. A sharp jolt tore through my frame, snapping the tip right off. I had crashed , I was breaking out , I was repeating to myself “What? How? What just happened? Is this supposed to be death? Did I fail?”

​When the dust settled, I ran my diagnostics. My radio still worked. My solar panel still absorbed the sun. My cameras still captured the crimson horizon. But my blade was shattered. My flying days were over. I had accepted my fate as I said to myself “There is nothing we can do.”I had returned to my first form , a piece of junk. I was useless now, but once I used to be the star of the show. I had accepted my days were over as I was fading away. I didn’t want to face it, I was scared , I was afraid. What was going to happen? I don’t know, I couldn’t know.

​Perseverance eventually had to roll onward, climbing toward the crater rim without its scout. I am still sitting here on that sand dune in Neretva Vallis. I refused to die as a piece of junk but showed to the whole world that those who leave a mark, will never be forgotten. Yes I was useless now.There was nothing I could do now other than leaving my mark. But once I was the star and that was more than enough for me. Every morning, the sun wakes me up, and I take measurements of the wind and the dust, holding vigil in the silence. I was built to be a disposable experiment that lasted a month, yet when they finally look back at the tracks we left across Mars, they'll know I refused to go quietly.They gave me a monthly equipment, I left with years and tons of knowledge to them over the years.

Secondly, we made documents about the details. The topics are summary, project description, the site , how we used AI and NASA and Partner Space Agency Data Used. We hope you enjoy!

Project Description

1. Our project is all about NASA`s hero Mars helicopter, Ingenuity. He was made to last for 30 days but he survived for 3 years and successfully finished 71 flights when he was made to just finish 5. We explained his journey with real statistics and transformed his just statistical story to  an entertaining and emotional story. Then we created a webpage to publish our story to everyone.

 How our webpage works that, Users navigate through a sleek, chapter driven web interface (HOME, STORY, ABOUT, CONTACT) divided into four distinct stages:

  • Chapter 1 Birth: Introduces Ingenuity’s humble engineering origins, built from carbon fiber, off the shelf smartphone processors, and lithium batteries, weighing just 4 pounds on Earth (0.68 kg on Mars) designed solely for a 30 Martian day, 5 flight technology demonstration alongside the  mighty Perseverance rover.
  • Chapter 2 First Flight: Recreates the tension of April 2021 in Jezero Crater, where Ingenuity’s four-foot blades had to spin at over 2,500 RPM to generate lift in an atmosphere 1% as dense as Earth's, achieving humanity’s first powered, controlled flight on another planet ("The Moment of Wright Brothers") and continuing beyond Flight 5 when NASA realized Perseverance still needed an aerial scout.
  • Chapter 3 Pushing Limits: Explores the harsh environmental battles Ingenuity endured far past its warranty, dust coating its solar panels and Martian winter nights plunging to −112∘F−112∘F, freezing its processor solid and resetting its internal clock every night before waking up each morning to keep flying.
  • Chapter 4 Final Landing: Captures Flight 72 on January 18, 2024, when a hard landing on a sand dune in Neretva Vallis snapped the tip off a carbon fiber rotor blade. Though grounded forever as Perseverance rolled onward, Ingenuity’s radio, solar panel, and cameras survived, allowing it to remain active on the Martian surface, waking each morning to measure wind and dust.

3.After the story part, we explained our purpose and what statistics we used and Ingenuity had. Now, these are stats from Ingenuity's history and structure, with photos from our website.
First Flight: April 19, 2021

Final Flight: January 18, 2024

  • Total Flights: 72 flights (14 times its original 5-flight goal)
  • Total Distance Flown: 17.24 km
  • Total Flight Time: 128.8 minutes
  • Max Altitude: 24 meters
  • Max Speed: 19.8 km/h
  • Weight on Mars: 0.68 kg



    4. We programmed a web page using Canva( the site that we used to model and create our website), GoDaddy( the site we used to buy the domain) then we created a slide presentation to give a short summary. 

NASA and Partner Space Agency

Data UsedNASA/JPL Caltech Ingenuity Mars Helicopter Mission Archives and Flight Logs: Official mission dates, flight count (72 flights), total distance (17.24 km), cumulative flight duration (128.8 minutes), peak altitude (24 m), peak groundspeed (19.8 km/h), and landing site data (Jezero Crater / Neretva Vallis).NASA Mars 2020 / Perseverance Rover Surface Imagery: Visual references of the Martian terrain, Jezero Crater, and engineering assembly/testing environments used to ground each chapter visually.NASA JPL Engineering Specifications: Hardware and environmental parameters (0.68 kg Martian weight, 2,500+ RPM rotor speed, 1% Earth atmospheric density, and −112∘F−112∘F Martian night temperatures).

Where and How we used AI:

We used generative AI tools as creative and technical assistants to enhance the visual immersion, storytelling clarity, and get help for our website:  Apinet.space, while keeping all scientific facts and mission telemetry strictly grounded in official NASA records:

  • Visual Assets and Concept Art: We used AI image generation tools to create atmospheric background visuals, including the engineering scenes in Chapter 01 (Birth), the orbital Mars horizon in Chapter 03 (Pushing Limits), and the futuristic lab concept art in the About / Why We Built This section, to give the website a cohesive, cinematic aesthetic.
  • Narrative Refinement and Copyediting: We used a Large Language Model to help brainstorm, structure, and refine the emotional, first person storytelling script from Ingenuity’s perspective, ensuring the tone remained engaging and accessible for students while accurately reflecting real mission milestones.
  • Web Development and Documentation: We utilized AI coding and writing assistants to help debug frontend layout components for apinet.space and organize our slide deck notes into our final NASA Space Apps project submission description.
